\chapter{Wind and Fire}
\label{ch:ta-wind-and-fire}
\hlchaptermodality{57}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the wind, sand, mud, smoke and an ember in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C57-ember and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kāṟṟu]{\ta{காற்று} (kāṟṟu) — the wind}

\label{lesson:TA-C57-wind}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{tēvaiyillai} mean, and what did \emph{ākaṭṭum} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{காற்று}}
\textbf{\ta{காற்று}} (\emph{kāṟṟu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the wind\textquotedblright{}.

Malayalam \ml{കാറ്റ്} (\emph{kāṟṟŭ}) is the same word with its ending worn shorter. Telugu takes \te{గాలి} (\emph{gāli}), which covers air as much as wind.

Tamil's word covers both too: the breeze coming through a doorway and the air inside a tyre are one word. What English splits into wind and air, Tamil leaves whole and lets the sentence decide.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things you can point at outdoors.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kāṟṟu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ākaṭṭum}, then \emph{kāṟṟu}, and let the doubled \ta{ற} hold
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{காற்று} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the wind\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maṇal]{\ta{மணல்} (maṇal) — sand}

\label{lesson:TA-C57-sand}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kāṟṟu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மணல்}}
\textbf{\ta{மணல்}} (\emph{maṇal}) — \textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{}.

Malayalam \ml{മണൽ} (\emph{maṇal}), letter for letter and sound for sound. Telugu goes somewhere else, to \emph{isuka}.

The \ta{ண} is the one made with the tongue curled back — the same letter you have just been doubling in \emph{kiṇṇam}. Here there is only one of them, so touch it once and move on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: what moves, and one of the things it moves.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maṇal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kāṟṟu}, then \emph{maṇal}, the wind and what it carries
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மணல்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sēṟu]{\ta{சேறு} (sēṟu) — mud}

\label{lesson:TA-C57-mud}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maṇal} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சேறு}}
\textbf{\ta{சேறு}} (\emph{sēṟu}) — \textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.

Wet earth churned up: the mud of a paddy field after rain, not dust and not clay. Here the three sisters go three ways — Malayalam \emph{ceḷi}, Telugu \emph{burada}, Tamil \ta{சேறு}.

Tamil keeps \emph{cakati} as well, for the thicker and dirtier kind. \ta{சேறு} is the working mud, the sort somebody walks into on purpose with a plough behind him.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: air, dry ground, and wet ground.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sēṟu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maṇal}, then \emph{sēṟu}, dry ground and wet
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{சேறு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pukai]{\ta{புகை} (pukai) — smoke}

\label{lesson:TA-C57-smoke}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sēṟu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{புகை}}
\textbf{\ta{புகை}} (\emph{pukai}) — \textquotedblleft{}smoke\textquotedblright{}.

Malayalam \ml{പുക} (\emph{puka}) is the same word one step shorter. Tamil's ends in the \emph{-ai} that so many of its everyday things end in: \emph{kiḷai}, \emph{kūṭai}, \emph{vitai}, and now this one.

\ta{புகை} is the smoke and also what somebody does over a cigarette. And when trains reached the Tamil country they were called \emph{pukaivaṇṭi}, the smoke vehicle, which is still what a great many people call them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one you can only see because of what it comes off.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pukai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sēṟu}, then \emph{pukai}, and let the \emph{-ai} open at the end
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{புகை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}smoke\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaṉal]{\ta{கனல்} (kaṉal) — an ember}

\label{lesson:TA-C57-ember}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pukai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கனல்}}
\textbf{\ta{கனல்}} (\emph{kaṉal}) — \textquotedblleft{}an ember\textquotedblright{}.

The live coal under the ash: fire with no flame on it. Malayalam has the word unchanged, \ml{കനൽ} (\emph{kanal}). Telugu's \te{నిప్పు} (\emph{nippu}) covers this and open fire together.

It is the word Tamil reaches for when it means heat held rather than heat let go. A \emph{kaṉal} in somebody's eye is anger they are keeping to themselves, and everyone in the room can tell.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Wind, sand, mud, smoke, and the coal under the ash.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaṉal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{kāṟṟu}, \emph{maṇal}, \emph{sēṟu}, \emph{pukai}, \emph{kaṉal}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{கனல்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an ember\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
